951.quote_or_event: “What good is social class and status? Truthfulness is measured within.”
951.explanation: In Majh ki Vaar, Guru Nanak denies that birth or social class counts for anything before God; what is tested is the truth a person carries inside.
951.tie_back: The Kural says rectitude and shame come naturally only to the well-born; Guru Nanak agrees that such qualities are what matter but places them in the person, not the family, much as Kalaignar's modern gloss does.
951.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 142, Raag Majh, Majh ki Vaar, salok of Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
951._accuracy_note: Partial and partly a counterpoint: Sikhism rejects birth and caste as the source of virtue, so it shares the Kural's values while disagreeing with the literal claim that they belong to good lineage.

952.quote_or_event: “Truth is higher than everything; but higher still is truthful living.”
952.explanation: In a Sri Raag hymn, Guru Nanak puts truthful conduct above even truth as an idea: what counts is a life that does not depart from it.
952.tie_back: The Kural says the well-born never slip from right conduct and truthfulness; Guru Nanak makes truthful living the highest of all.
952.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 62, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
952._accuracy_note: A strong fit on truth and conduct; the Kural's third quality, shame, is not named, and Gurbani ties the ideal to the person rather than to family.

953.quote_or_event: “Do not utter even a single harsh word; your True Lord and Master abides in all. Do not break anyone's heart; these are all priceless jewels.”
953.explanation: Sheikh Farid, included in the Granth, forbids harsh speech and wounding anyone, because God lives in every person and each is a priceless jewel.
953.tie_back: Two of the Kural's four marks, kind words and never belittling others, are exactly what Farid asks for, and he gives a reason: God is in everyone.
953.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok Sheikh Farid (salok 129) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
953._accuracy_note: A strong fit on pleasant speech and not scorning others; the cheerful face and generosity of the Kural's list are not mentioned, and lineage plays no part.

954.quote_or_event: “To take what rightfully belongs to another, is like a Muslim eating pork, or a Hindu eating beef.”
954.explanation: In Majh ki Vaar, Guru Nanak says that taking what is not rightfully one's own is as forbidden as the strongest food taboo of each community.
954.tie_back: The Kural says the noble will not do anything base even for crores of wealth; Guru Nanak makes ill-gotten gain something to recoil from absolutely.
954.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 141, Raag Majh, Majh ki Vaar, salok of Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
954._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the verse concerns one kind of debasing gain, taking another's due, and grounds the refusal in conscience before God rather than family honour.

955.quote_or_event: “One who works for what he eats, and gives some of what he has - O Nanak, he knows the Path.”
955.explanation: Guru Nanak sums up the householder ideal: earn by honest labour (kirat karni) and share some of whatever one has (vand chhakna), however little it is.
955.tie_back: The Kural says the old, worthy family keeps its generous nature even when its means shrink; Guru Nanak asks every earner to give 'some' of what he has, which holds in poverty as in plenty.
955.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1245, Raag Saarang, Saarang ki Vaar, salok of Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
955._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on giving that does not depend on wealth; the verse does not speak of decline into poverty, and it applies to everyone rather than to an ancient family.

956.quote_or_event: “One knows the Truth only when the Truth is in his heart. The filth of falsehood departs, and the body is washed clean.”
956.explanation: In Asa di Vaar, Guru Nanak says truth is real only when it lives in the heart, and then the stain of falsehood is washed away.
956.tie_back: The Kural speaks of those who resolve to live true to a spotless line and never stoop to deceit; Guru Nanak locates that spotlessness in a heart cleansed of falsehood.
956.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 468, Raag Aasaa, Asa di Vaar, salok of Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
956._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both reject deceit and prize stainlessness, but Guru Nanak's purity is inward and has nothing to do with family line.

957.quote_or_event: When Aurangzeb questioned Ram Rai, the elder son of Guru Har Rai, about a line of the Adi Granth he thought disparaging to Muslims, Ram Rai tried to appease the emperor by suggesting the line had been wrongly written. Guru Har Rai excommunicated him for this and later named his younger son, Har Krishan, as successor instead.
957.explanation: A single compromise by the Guru's own son, made at the imperial court, became a defining event, and he was passed over for the succession.
957.tie_back: The Kural says a fault in someone of high birth shows like the spot on the moon; Ram Rai's lapse, made in the most public place by the son of the Guru, could not be hidden or overlooked.
957._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on how a high position magnifies a fault; Sikh tradition draws from it the lesson that the Guruship goes by faithfulness, not birth.

958.quote_or_event: “His sons did not obey His Word; they turned their backs on Him as Guru.”
958.explanation: In their Vaar in Raag Ramkali, the bards Satta and Balwand recall that Guru Nanak's own sons would not accept his choice, so he installed his disciple Lehna as Guru Angad instead.
958.tie_back: The Kural says that a lack of love in someone who seems good makes people doubt his lineage; the Granth records that Guru Nanak's sons, lacking that devotion, lost the inheritance to a disciple who had it.
958.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 967, Raag Ramkali, Ramkali ki Vaar of Satta and Balwand (tr. BaniDB English)
958._accuracy_note: A strong fit on conduct calling a birthright into question, though Sikhism goes further than the Kural by transferring the inheritance itself to a non-relative; the English is the BaniDB translation, as the API shows no Sant Singh Khalsa line here.

959.quote_or_event: “O Nanak, speaking insipid words, the body and mind become insipid.”
959.explanation: In Asa di Vaar, Guru Nanak teaches that harsh, loveless speech both shows and shapes the state of a person's whole being.
959.tie_back: The Kural says a person's words reveal what they come from as a sprout reveals its soil; Guru Nanak says one's words reveal, and even make, what one is.
959.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 473, Raag Aasaa, Asa di Vaar, salok of Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
959._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: both link speech to inner nature, but Guru Nanak ties it to the speaker's own character rather than to the family.

960.quote_or_event: “Sweetness and humility, O Nanak, are the essence of virtue and goodness.”
960.explanation: In Asa di Vaar, Guru Nanak names sweetness of speech and humility (nimrata) as the sum of all good qualities.
960.tie_back: The Kural closes by saying that one who wants a noble name must be humble towards everyone; Guru Nanak makes humility the essence of goodness itself.
960.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 470, Raag Aasaa, Asa di Vaar, salok of Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
960._accuracy_note: A strong fit on humility as the way to true standing; the Kural's pairing with shame is not mirrored, and Gurbani seeks goodness, not family name.
